frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, NTDS.dit extraction, credential dumping tool execution, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or credential stores, no suspicious registry hive or NTDS.dit access, and no anomalous authentication events consistent with stolen credentials.

verdict.rationale: 5 in-scope incident(s) of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium): I01 T1003.001 (F01, F02, F11, F15, F23, F31, F32, F33), I02 T1552.001 (F27, F52), I03 T1552.001 (F53), I04 T1552.004 (F26, F49, F51), I05 T1557.001 (F37)
verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Malicious PowerShell (PID 2976, spawned by control.exe with hidden window and obfuscated bitmap-decoded IEX payload) opened full-access handles to lsass.exe (0x1f3fff, 0x1fffff) and Security 4663 recorded 'Read from process memory' on lsass.exe by pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: Sysmon event 10 shows PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) accessing lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff; Security 4663 confirms 'Read from process memory' on lsass.exe by the same process/user.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: No reg save/SAM/SECURITY command lines, no Sysmon event 2 hive access, and no 4663 access to SAM/SECURITY registry keys.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No NTDS.dit file access, ntdsutil/vssadmin/shadow-copy activity in Sysmon, Security 4688 or PowerShell 4104 logs.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: The only LSA secret reads (4662, Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC, mask 0x2) are routine queries by NT AUTHORITY\LOCAL SERVICE, not adversary LSA-secret dumping.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No 4663/4656 access to SECURITY/Cache registry keys and no PowerShell script blocks referencing cache/dcc2/mimikatz.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No Security 4929 replication events and no drsuapi/lsadump/dcsync/Get-ADReplAccount references in process creation or PowerShell logs.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only capture-like activity is Microsoft Azure Network Watcher's netsh trace start/stop on scranton.dmevals.local, spawned by NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service as SYSTEM using the signed Microsoft netsh.exe. No Npcap/WinPcap/dumpcap/Wireshark binaries, drivers, files or registry keys exist in sysmon or security; the 7045 service installs are PSEXESVC and a Java service, not capture drivers; the zeek window shows only normal protocol logs and self-signed-cert notices. No adversary network sniffing observed.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: LSASS credential-memory access (0x1f3fff/0x1fffff) by pbeesly via PowerShell on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua, plus a PowerShell credential toolkit (Invoke-Discovery, Get-PrivateKeys).

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No keylogging indicators: no GetAsyncKeyState/SetWindowsHookEx/RegisterHotKey script blocks, no hook/keylogger registry keys, no keylogger service installed.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Only legitimate consent.exe UAC prompts; no fake credential-prompt executables or GUI input capture observed.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No IIS/w3wp/appcmd processes, no wwwroot/inetpub/login file or object access; Zeek HTTP limited to WebDAV file transfers.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe (scranton) and wsmprovhost.exe (nashua) opened lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff including 'Read from process memory', consistent with credential API access/hooking.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625 failed-logon events in windows.security (count total 0); no brute-force tooling in sysmon process stacks. WMI 5857/5858 hits are routine RSOP DeleteInstance by SYSTEM.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons and no guessing tools. PowerShell 4104 hits are credential theft/exfil scripts (Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-Exfil) and PsExec with a plaintext password, i.e. credential use, not guessing.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No hashcat/john/wordlist command lines (C104 zero hits); LSASS access is svchost.exe 0x1000 (normal); no cracking output files.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No 4625 events and no burst of failed authentications across accounts; only successful 4624/4634 logons.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed logons and no source.ip tied to authentication failures; only successful logons present.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smartcard interception activity found. The only smartcard artifact is the Microsoft-signed SmartcardCredentialProvider.dll loaded by LogonUI.exe (legitimate Windows component). All 'Credential'/'Ngc' registry writes are routine OS service registration by services.exe/svchost.exe. The 4648 explicit-credential logons are PsExec lateral movement (pbeesly -> NASHUA), not MFA interception. No fake credential provider, interception DLL, or MFA-related process/file was observed.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: No forced-authentication artifacts found. Outbound SMB (445/139) is exclusively from process.executable 'System' to the DC 10.0.0.4 / link-local IPv6, i.e. normal domain/GPO traffic; share access is machine-account SYSVOL reads plus pbeesly's PsExec lateral movement (ADMIN$/IPC$, PSEXESVC.exe, svcctl, samr). No .scf/.searchconnector-ms/WebDAV coercion files (only benign Explorer Recent .lnk and a StartUp hostui.lnk), and no WebDAV/NTLM coercion script blocks (C135 zero hits).

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opened lsass with 0x1F3FFF — full-access handles to LSASS memory, the credential-dumping primitive, within an APT29-style intrusion (SeaDuke stage, javamtsup service, PsExec).

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No browser cookie store was accessed, copied or exfiltrated. Queries for cookie/Login Data/WebCache/Local State filenames in Sysmon file-create (11), file-create-time (2), process command lines (1) and PowerShell 4104 scriptblocks all returned zero hits. The only browser process accesses (Sysmon 10) are from Explorer.EXE and svchost.exe with low granted access (0x2000/0x3000), i.e. normal shell/COM behaviour. The real malicious activity on these hosts is a PsExec-based credential-access/lateral-movement campaign, which is not T1539.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Unsecured credentials observed: plaintext password in PsExec command line and hardcoded passwords in PowerShell scripts on scranton.dmevals.local.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Plaintext credentials in PsExec command lines (Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) and hardcoded WebDAV exfil credentials (MyCozyPassw0rd!) in PowerShell scripts.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: No reg query/save/export of SAM/SECURITY/LSA and no 4663 access to credential hives; only routine lsass.exe cached-credential writes.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: All ConsoleHost_history/PSReadLine/history checks returned zero hits across powershell, sysmon and security datasets.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys script exported all LocalMachine certificates with private keys to .pfx files on scranton; a .pfx was written to Downloads.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: SYSVOL/GroupPolicy DataStore file creations were routine svchost.exe GPO processing; no Groups.xml/cpassword activity.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: Hidden PowerShell (PID 2976, spawned by control.exe) opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF on scranton, and wsmprovhost.exe opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF on nashua — full-access LSASS reads consistent with credential-store dumping.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: Rar.exe used to password-protect staged data on nashua, then wiped with sdelete; consistent with credential/data staging though no browser store access observed.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: The LSASS-dumping PowerShell was launched via control.exe LOLbin with a hidden, EP-bypass command line decoding a steganographic payload from monkey.png; LSASS is the memory store for Windows Credential Manager/DPAPI vault secrets.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No password-manager (1Password/KeePass/LastPass/Bitwarden/kdbx) file, process or script artifacts found in any dataset.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: LSASS was opened with full access (0x1fffff/0x1f3fff) by PowerShell.exe on scranton and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua, indicating credential theft from the authentication process; however this is memory access (T1003.001), not modification of the auth process, so the T1556 family itself is not confirmed.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: No DC authentication patching: LSASS access is dominated by svchost/antimalware/telemetry with 0x1000, and no unsigned DLL loads into LSASS or lsass/cryptdll service installs were found.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No Notification Packages registry change, no PasswordFilter script, no .dll service install, no DLL drop into System32/SysWOW64.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No reversible-encryption references in scripts, command lines, service installs, or account-policy events (4739 zero hits).

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No account-policy change (4739) and no AD authentication policy cmdlets observed.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No directory-service object modification events (5136/5137/5141 zero hits).

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No network provider DLL registration or LSA registry modification observed.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: Relay-style python tooling and NTLM network logon observed, but no single dataset shows a complete AiTM chain; Zeek and Windows windows do not overlap.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe spawned by PSEXESVC.exe on nashua made 348 connections to 192.168.0.4:8443, with an NTLM network logon for pbeesly and SMB/NBT-NS traffic present.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: One responder MAC dominates Zeek conn records, but no corroborating ARP-cache evidence on Windows hosts.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP (67/68) traffic, DHCP server events, or DHCP/netsh command lines in any dataset.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: No Kerberos ticket theft/forgery indicators in any dataset. All ticket requests use AES256 (0x12), no RC4 downgrade, no anomalous SPN or privilege logons. The credential access present (LSASS access 0x1FFFFF by PowerShell on scranton) is T1003 memory dumping, not a T1558 technique.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: No RC4 TGS requests and no anomalous 4672 special-privilege logons; all 4672 events are legitimate machine/system accounts (NEWYORK$, SYSTEM, pbeesly, SCRANTON$).

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: All 4769 service-ticket requests use AES256 (0x12) and target only normal machine/service accounts (krbtgt, NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$); no forged silver-ticket indicators.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: Every TGS request (windows.security 4769 and Zeek kerberos) uses AES256; no RC4 (0x17) service tickets and no SPN-enumeration/kerberoasting tooling in PowerShell command lines.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All 4768 AS-REQ events have win.PreAuthType 2 (preauth enabled); no preauth-disabled accounts and no AS-REP roasting tooling observed.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: Only cookie-related activity is the legitimate Windows WebDAV client (davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie via WebClient svchost) and an OS INetCookies file; the PowerShell 'cookie/token' hit is a benign Sysinternals readme.ps1. No forging tooling.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Web cookie events are normal WebDAV client cookie setting and OS INetCookies creation by svchost; no browser cookie theft or cookie forging observed.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Zero hits for SAML/Assertion/ADFS/JWT/NotOnOrAfter across powershell, windows.other and sysmon; zeek TLS server_name shows only 192.168.0.4, no SSO/ADFS endpoint.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA request generation activity found. Searches for MFA/2FA/Authenticator/OTP keywords in windows.other messages, PowerShell 4104 script blocks, sysmon process command lines and process executables returned no MFA tooling. No 4625 failed logons. Authentication events are ordinary Windows/RDP logons (1149/21 for pbeesly from 172.18.39.2), NTLM-in-use info (6038) and Credential Guard config (14). External connections to login.live.com and Microsoft/Azure CDN IPs come from svchost.exe, backgroundTaskHost.exe and BackgroundTransferHost.exe (normal OS telemetry).

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: Certificate theft via Get-PrivateKeys exporting LocalMachine certs with private keys to .pfx files on scranton.

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll, etc.) by rare executable names.
Find processes opening handles to LSASS (Sysmon Event 10) which is the core signal of OS credential dumping.

args.query: FROM windows.powershell METADATA _id, _index | WHERE TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*set-aduser*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*set-adaccount*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*set-adauthenticationpolicy*" OR TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*set-aduser*" OR TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*set-adauthenticationpolicy*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.command_line, win.ScriptBlockText, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Look for PowerShell modifying AD user/authentication policy objects (MFA attributes disabled) per ATT&CK log source 'Set-ADUser or Set-ADAuthenticationPolicy with MFA attributes disabled'.
EventCode 4739 (domain policy changed) is the ATT&CK-listed Security event for MFA policy modification; count shows whether any policy change occurred.
If 4739 exists, stack by subject to see which account changed domain policy.
windows.other carries AD/DS and directory-service events; check for policy/account-change records that could reflect MFA policy tampering.

args.query: event.code:1 AND (process.command_line:*Set-ADUser* OR process.command_line:*Set-ADAuthenticationPolicy* OR process.command_line:*dsacls* OR process.command_line:*ntdsutil*)

checks.purpose: Stack process images whose command lines touch AD user/authentication policy objects.
EventCode 5136 (directory service object modified) is the ATT&CK-listed source for hybrid-identity backdooring of on-prem objects.
If 5136 exists, stack by object type to spot modifications to user/identity objects.
Stack logon processes for anomalous logons without MFA enforcement (e.g. unexpected process names).
EventCode 7 image loads: stack loaded modules to find authentication/identity DLLs loaded by unusual processes (hybrid identity patching).

findings.title: OS credential dumping activity via LSASS handle from malicious PowerShell
findings.summary: The overarching OS Credential Dumping activity is present on scranton.dmevals.local: the compromised PowerShell loader (PID 2976, spawned by control.exe with hidden window and obfuscated payload) requested full-access handles to lsass.exe (0x1f3fff, 0x1fffff) and Security 4663 recorded 'Read from process memory' on lsass.exe by user pbeesly. No other credential-store dumping (SAM/NTDS/LSA secrets/DCSync) was observed.

findings.title: Malicious PowerShell reads LSASS memory with full-access handle on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, a PowerShell process (PID 2976) launched by control.exe with a hidden window and an obfuscated bitmap-decoded IEX payload opened a handle to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (full-access, dump-capable masks) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z. Windows Security event 4663 corroborates the same process (user pbeesly, logon 0x372E81) accessing lsass.exe with 'Read from process memory'. This is consistent with LSASS credential dumping by the APT29-style PowerShell framework (which also ran keystroke logging, screen capture and exfil functions).

findings.title: Input capture family: LSASS credential access dominates; no keylogging/GUI/web capture
findings.summary: Across the T1056 family, the only malicious input/credential-capture activity is API-level access to LSASS credential memory (T1056.004) by pbeesly via PowerShell on scranton and via wsmprovhost on nashua, alongside a PowerShell credential toolkit (Invoke-Discovery, Get-PrivateKeys exporting cert private keys). The high-volume Sysmon 10 process-access events are otherwise dominated by benign svchost.exe/backgroundTaskHost.exe/Explorer.EXE accesses with GrantedAccess 0x1000, and the 4656/4663 object accesses are dominated by routine registry reads (Session Manager\Environment, Control\Lsa, Winlogon). No keylogging, GUI input capture, or web portal capture was observed.

findings.title: PowerShell and wsmprovhost open LSASS with full access (credential API access) on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02, user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran a PowerShell credential-access toolkit (script path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) that included Invoke-Discovery and Get-PrivateKeys (exporting certificate private keys with password 'saribas'). At 03:05:16 PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, including 'Read from process memory'), and the corresponding Security 4656 handle request confirms AccessMask 0x1f3fff against \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe. On nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29, wsmprovhost.exe (remote PowerShell, PID 0x1e28) as pbeesly requested AccessMask 0x1f3fff on lsass.exe. This is direct API-level access to LSASS credential memory, consistent with credential API hooking/dumping rather than normal system behaviour.

findings.title: PowerShell and remote WMI host processes opened lsass with full access (credential dumping primitive) during APT29-style intrusion
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02, in an intrusion using the pbeesly account and SeaDuke tooling, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:16Z, and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) on nashua.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29Z. These full-access handles to lsass are the standard primitive for reading credential material from LSASS memory, matching the T1212 credential-access hypothesis. The activity is part of a broader APT29-style chain: a Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service installed via javamtsup.exe on scranton, PsExec/PSEXESVC service installs on nashua, and PowerShell script blocks Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA and Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA. The remaining lsass accesses (svchost.exe 0x1000, Azure AntimalwareConfig/Telemetry 0x1400, wininit/csrss at boot) are normal system behaviour.

On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly repeatedly invoked PsExec64.exe with the account password supplied in cleartext on the command line: "C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\PsExec64.exe" -accepteula \\NASHUA -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe. Four such executions were observed between 2020-05-02T03:11:18Z and 03:14:42Z, targeting host NASHUA and launching C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe. The credential is stored in the process command line (recoverable from process listings/logs), matching unsecured credentials in files/command lines. Corroborating PowerShell script blocks on the same host (Invoke-Exfil) also embed a plaintext password ("MyCozyPassw0rd!") for a WebDAV share.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script block (Event 4104, ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) defining function Get-PrivateKeys. A matching Sysmon file-creation event confirms the exported key material: C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by powershell.exe at 2020-05-02T03:04:57Z. This is direct theft of private keys/certificates from the local machine store.

LSASS handle access with full access rights by PowerShell/WinRM — credential dumping, not auth-process modification
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:16, and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, WinRM remote PowerShell, parent svchost.exe) on nashua.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29. PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates with private keys to .pfx files
findings.summary: On host scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell script block defining function Get-PrivateKeys (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1). The function enumerates every certificate under cert:\LocalMachine recursively, and for each certificate with a Thumbprint calls Export-PfxCertificate to write a password-protected .pfx (password 'saribas') into $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads with a random filename. This is direct theft of authentication certificates and their private keys. The export materialized on disk: Sysmon event 11 shows powershell.exe (PID 3876) creating C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 2020-05-02T03:04:57.460Z, matching the script's random-filename pattern. A follow-up script block Invoke-BeachCleanup (ScriptBlock ID 31f21f1d-9199-4d21-9ea8-...) deletes $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.pfx (along with *.bmp, *.png and %APPDATA%\OfficeSupplies.7z), consistent with anti-forensic cleanup of the stolen certificate material. The activity is attributed to the apt29-powershell hunt source and mordorDataset tags.

findings.title: netsh trace capture on scranton.dmevals.local is Azure Network Watcher agent activity, not adversary sniffing
findings.summary: The only packet-capture-looking activity in the environment is `netsh.exe trace start capture=yes` (and the matching `trace stop`) on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z / 03:19:24Z. Both invocations were spawned by the Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent (parent image C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service) running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, writing to a TEMP .etl file. The netsh.exe binary is the Microsoft-signed system binary (Company: Microsoft Corporation, OriginalFileName: netsh.exe, FileVersion 10.0.18362.1). The only .lnk files created (Sysmon 11) are benign Explorer 'Recent' shortcuts and a hostui.lnk in the StartUp folder written by powershell.exe (persistence), not .scf/.searchconnector-ms/WebDAV coercion files. findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and zeek there is no evidence of Kerberos ticket theft or forgery. All TGS/AS ticket requests in windows.security (4769/4768) and all Zeek kerberos records use AES256 (0x12 / aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96) only, with no RC4 (0x17) downgrade, no anomalous SPN enumeration and no AS-REQ without preauth. The 4672 special-privilege logons are all normal machine/system accounts (NEWYORK$, SYSTEM, pbeesly, SCRANTON$). The only credential-access activity found is LSASS process-memory access by PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, which is credential dumping (T1003), not a T1558 technique.
findings.title: No Kerberos ticket theft/forgery observed; credential access present is LSASS memory dumping (T1003)

findings.summary: Golden ticket forging would show RC4 (0x17) TGS requests and/or special-privilege (4672) logons for accounts that should not hold them. All 28 4769 events use TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256) for pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL only, and the 212 4672 events are all for legitimate machine/system accounts (NEWYORK$ 123, SYSTEM 59, pbeesly 19, SCRANTON$ 4, DWM-1/2, NASHUA$, NETWORK SERVICE, LOCAL SERVICE). No forged-ticket indicators.
findings.title: No Golden Ticket activity: no RC4 TGS, no anomalous 4672 privilege logons

findings.summary: Silver ticket forging would produce service-ticket (4769) requests with RC4 encryption or for services/accounts not normally accessed. All 4769 events use AES256 (0x12) and target only pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL for services krbtgt, NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$ and WEC$ — normal machine/service account access. No RC4 service tickets and no anomalous service targets.

findings.summary: Kerberoasting requires requesting service tickets with weak RC4 (0x17) encryption to crack offline. Every 4769 TGS request in windows.security uses TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256), and every Zeek kerberos TGS record uses aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96. No RC4 service tickets and no SPN enumeration tooling (no setspn/GetUserSPNs/Rubeus/Invoke-Kerberoast in PowerShell command lines).

findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other there is no evidence of forged web credentials. The only cookie-related activity is the legitimate Windows WebDAV client: on scranton.dmevals.local, rundll32.exe running davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie for http://192.168.0.4/webdav, spawned by the WebClient service (svchost.exe -k LocalService -p -s WebClient) under user pbeesly. A single INetCookies file was created by svchost in a ServiceProfiles path (normal OS behavior). The lone PowerShell 4104 'cookie/token' hit is a benign Sysinternals readme.ps1 script (Get-AttributesMask). The 4648 explicit-credential logons are PsExec (C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe) lateral movement by pbeesly, i.e. credential use, not forging. No SAML/JWT/ADFS artifacts anywhere.

findings.title: Web cookie activity is legitimate WebDAV client and OS INetCookies, not forging
findings.summary: The only cookie-related events are the Windows WebDAV client setting an auth cookie (rundll32.exe davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie for http://192.168.0.4/webdav, parent svchost WebClient service) on scranton.dmevals.local as pbeesly, and a single INetCookies file created by svchost under a ServiceProfiles package path. findings.title: No SAML token forging artifacts observed
findings.summary: No SAML/Assertion/ADFS/JWT artifacts were found in any dataset. Searches for SAML, Assertion, NotOnOrAfter, ADFS, token and cert in PowerShell script blocks, windows.other messages, and sysmon process command lines returned zero hits. The zeek TLS server_name stack shows only 192.168.0.4 (no SSO/ADFS endpoint). No evidence of SAML token forging.

findings.title: No MFA request generation activity; authentication events are normal Windows/RDP logons
findings.summary: Hunting for T1621 (Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation) across windows.other, windows.powershell, windows.security and windows.sysmon found no MFA tooling, no repeated authentication-prompt generation, and no identity-provider abuse. The only authentication-related events are ordinary Windows behaviour: an RDP logon by user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local (TerminalServices events 1149/21 from source 172.18.39.2), an NTLM-in-use informational event (6038), and a Credential Guard configuration event (14). DNS/network activity to login.live.com and Microsoft/Azure CDN IPs originates from svchost.exe, backgroundTaskHost.exe and BackgroundTransferHost.exe (normal OS telemetry). No 4625 failed logons and no MFA/authenticator/OTP processes or command lines were observed.

findings.title: Certificate store registry modifications (4657) are benign OS/Sysmon activity
findings.summary: The 4657 registry-value-modification hits touching certificate paths are not attacker certificate theft. The single SystemCertificates hit is on nashua.dmevals.local where the modifying process is C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe (PID 0xd64) under the machine account NASHUA$ (S-1-5-18, logon 0x3E7), modifying the ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656 Blob — normal certificate-store maintenance by a system process. The remaining 4657 hits are wevtutil.exe (SCRANTON$) editing WMI Autologger EventLog-Application keys, unrelated to certificates. The Sysmon registry-set (event 13) hits under SystemCertificates/Cryptography are likewise routine certificate-store and CryptoAPI symbolic-link writes. None of these show an adversary exporting or forging authentication certificates.

incidents.title: LSASS memory credential dumping via hidden PowerShell on scranton
incidents.rationale: All these findings describe the same attacker action: a hidden, obfuscated PowerShell process (PID 2976, spawned by control.exe, user pbeesly) on scranton.dmevals.local opening lsass.exe with full-access masks (0x1f3fff, 0x1fffff) and 'Read from process memory' (Security 4663), plus the same primitive via wsmprovhost.exe on nashua. This is credential dumping from LSASS memory, best fitting T1003.001 (LSASS Memory).

incidents.title: Plaintext credentials in PsExec command lines for lateral movement to NASHUA
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe the same action: PsExec64.exe invoked four times from scranton with the cleartext password 'Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by' for dmevals\pbeesly on \\NASHUA, launching C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe. Credentials exposed in process command lines fit T1552.001 (Credentials In Files).

incidents.title: Hardcoded WebDAV exfil credentials in Invoke-Exfil script
incidents.rationale: The Invoke-Exfil PowerShell script (psversion.ps1) compresses the Downloads folder to OfficeSupplies.7z and copies it to a WebDAV share using hardcoded plaintext credentials ('cozy' / 'MyCozyPassw0rd!'). Hardcoded credentials in a script fit T1552.001 (Credentials In Files).

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys exports LocalMachine certificate private keys to .pfx on scranton
incidents.rationale: These findings all describe the same action: the PowerShell function Get-PrivateKeys (from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and exporting every certificate with its private key to password-protected .pfx files (e.g. coyn5igj.3io.pfx) in the user's Downloads folder. This is theft of private keys, best fitting T1552.004 (Private Keys).

incidents.title: Python relay/listener tooling on nashua with NTLM network logon
incidents.rationale: C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe launched by PSEXESVC.exe making 348 outbound TCP connections to 192.168.0.4:8443, with SMB/NBT-NS traffic and an NTLM network logon, is consistent with SMB relay/name-resolution poisoning, best fitting T1557.001 (Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay).

incidents.title: Single responder MAC for most Zeek connections (possible L2 redirection)
incidents.rationale: A single responder MAC answering for most Zeek connections could reflect ARP cache poisoning, but the MAC is a synthetic placeholder and no corroborating evidence exists; best fit is T1557.002 (ARP Cache Poisoning), assessed suspicious/low confidence.

incidents.title: csc.exe compiles attacker DLLs from PowerShell on scranton
incidents.rationale: powershell.exe invoking csc.exe to compile attacker source into DLLs is on-host payload compilation, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1027 (Obfuscated Files or Information).

incidents.title: Python interpreter dropped in Temp and launched via PsExec on nashua
incidents.rationale: C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe launched by PSEXESVC.exe is attacker tool execution, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter).

incidents.title: accesschk.exe permission reconnaissance on scranton
incidents.rationale: Sysinternals accesschk.exe launched by powershell.exe is permission reconnaissance, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1069 (Permission Groups Discovery).

incidents.title: SDelete anti-forensics wiping of payload and staged archives on scranton
incidents.rationale: sdelete64.exe securely wiping the .scr payload, Draft.Zip and SysinternalsSuite.zip is indicator removal/anti-forensics, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1070 (Indicator Removal).

incidents.title: Malicious .scr payload in ProgramData launched by explorer on scranton
incidents.rationale: A .scr executable in C:\ProgramData\victim launched by explorer.exe is user execution of a malicious file, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1204 (User Execution).

incidents.title: hostui.exe LOLbin launched by PowerShell on scranton
incidents.rationale: hostui.exe launched by powershell.exe is abuse of a legitimate signed binary as a LOLbin, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1218 (System Binary Proxy Execution).

incidents.title: sdclt.exe LOLbin launched by cmd.exe on scranton
incidents.rationale: sdclt.exe launched by cmd.exe and spawning control.exe is LOLbin abuse, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1218 (System Binary Proxy Execution).

incidents.title: Rar.exe password-protected staging and sdelete wiping on nashua
incidents.rationale: Rar.exe creating a password-protected archive of collected data and sdelete64.exe wiping it is collection/archive staging and anti-forensics, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1560 (Archive Collected Data).

FROM logs-windows.sysmon-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "10" AND win.TargetImage LIKE "*lsass*" AND process.executable LIKE "*PowerShell*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, process.executable, win.SourceImage, win.GrantedAccess, win.CallTrace, _id, _index | SORT @timestamp ASC

FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "4104" OR event.code == "4103" | WHERE TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*lsass*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*mimikatz*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*kerberos*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*ticket*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*krbtgt*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*sekurlsa*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*invoke-*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, event.code, win.ScriptBlockText, process.command_line, _id, _index | SORT @timestamp ASC

FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE @timestamp >= "2020-05-02T03:04:50" AND @timestamp <= "2020-05-02T03:06:00" AND host.name == "scranton.dmevals.local" | KEEP @timestamp, event.code, win.ScriptBlockText, process.command_line, _id, _index | SORT @timestamp ASC
FROM logs-windows.security-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "4769" | STATS cnt = COUNT(*) BY win.TicketEncryptionType, win.TargetUserName | SORT cnt DESC
FROM logs-windows.security-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "4672" | STATS cnt = COUNT(*) BY user.name | SORT cnt DESC
FROM logs-zeek-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.action == "kerberos" | STATS cnt = COUNT(*) BY zeek.cipher, zeek.request_type, zeek.service | SORT cnt DESC
FROM logs-windows.sysmon-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "10" AND win.TargetImage LIKE "*lsass*" | STATS c = COUNT(*) BY win.SourceImage, host.name | SORT c DESC | LIMIT 30
FROM logs-windows.sysmon-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "11" AND file.path LIKE "*Cookie*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, file.path, process.executable, user.name, _id, _index

FROM logs-windows.sysmon-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "1" AND (process.command_line LIKE "*cookie*" OR process.command_line LIKE "*Cookie*" OR process.command_line LIKE "*SAML*" OR process.command_line LIKE "*jwt*" OR process.command_line LIKE "*adfs*" OR process.command_line LIKE "*ADFS*" OR process.command_line LIKE "*token*") | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, process.executable, process.command_line, user.name, _id, _index | LIMIT 30

FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "4104" AND (win.ScriptBlockText LIKE "*cookie*" OR win.ScriptBlockText LIKE "*Cookie*" OR win.ScriptBlockText LIKE "*SAML*" OR win.ScriptBlockText LIKE "*jwt*" OR win.ScriptBlockText LIKE "*Set-Cookie*" OR win.ScriptBlockText LIKE "*session*") | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, win.Path, user.name, _id, _index | LIMIT 30

FROM logs-windows.sysmon-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "1" AND process.executable LIKE "*rundll32*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, process.executable, process.command_line, process.parent.executable, process.parent.command_line, user.name, _id, _index | LIMIT 30
